paper_title: World-in-Context: Interactive Video World Modeling with In-Context Conditioning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion. Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly. In this work, we present World-in-Context, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC). Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways, World-in-Context unifies view, action, and camera controls into explicit tokens contextualized directly within a shared self-attention space. Our formulation reveals that (i) explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting dynamics and unlock emergent view switching from single-view data, while (ii) action and camera inputs play complementary roles in governing local responsiveness and global stability. To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions. On WBench, World-in-Context-5B achieves navigation performance on par with 22B EchoWM ($81.5$ vs. $81.6$) and attains a $93.8\%$ perspective-switching success rate, substantially outperforming existing 5B baselines ($18.8\%$). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages of World-in-Context under richer conditioning mixtures, favorable data efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion. Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly. In this work, we present World-in-Context, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC). Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways, World-in-Context unifies view, action, and camera controls into explicit tokens contextualized directly within shared self-attention space. Our formulation reveals that (i) explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting dynamics and unlock emergent view switching from single-view data, while (ii) action and camera inputs play complementary roles in governing local responsiveness and global stability. To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions. On WBench, World-in-Context-5B achieves navigation performance on par with 22B EchoWM (81.5 vs. 81.6) and attains 93.8% perspective-switching success rate, substantially outperforming existing 5B baselines (18.8%). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages of World-in-Context under richer conditioning mixtures, favorable data efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts. 1. Introduction Video generation has rapidly advanced from passive video generation [10, 22, 41] toward interactive world models [9, 38, 40, 45], empowering users to actively steer dynamic visual environments. In this paradigm, the model acts as an interactive simulator where users provide control inputs to navigate and explore the environment, while the model dynami1 cally predicts the evolving visual observations in response. At its core, effectively simulating such an interactive world hinges on two fundamental dimensions [28, 43]: ➀ how the world is viewed across distinct perspectives, and ➁ how user inputs concurrently govern character dynamics and camera viewports. Together, these dimensions define how an agent actively perceives and intervenes in an unfolding generative world. Despite recent progress [15, 39, 40, 55, 59], current interactive pipelines often overlook the systematic formulation of these two essential dimensions: ❶ viewmode ambiguity: first- (FPP) and third-person (TPP) perspectives increasingly appear in interactive data, yet view mode is often specified only implicitly through text captions [9, 38, 39, 55], while free-camera (FREE) roaming is frequently conflated with FPP control despite their different motion semantics; and ❷ action-camera entanglement: most pipelines rely primarily on continuous camera trajectories alone for control [13, 31, 39, 55], overlooking the distinct role of discrete actions, especially in third-person interaction where character and camera motion form separate degrees of freedom. naive remedy would be simply attaching auxiliary condition channels for each missing signal. However, existing paradigms [9, 19, 33, 40, 45, 56] typically accommodate interactive controls through separate modules (e.g., AdaLN modulation), which tends to isolate different control signals and leaves their cross-dependencies to be captured only indirectly, as shown in Figure 2 (Left). As interaction becomes richer and more compositional, coordinating these modular branches grows increasingly intricate, especially when the interpretation of one signal inherently depends on concurrent inputs and the active viewport. In this work, we propose World-in-Context, which unifies multi-dimensional interaction through an InContext Conditioning (ICC) paradigm. Rather than routing controls into isolated architectural branches, World-in-Context casts diverse interactive signals into token sequences and prepends them directly into the shared self-attention space alongside visual latents. Within this unified interface, we revisit the aforementioned limitations along two fronts: Explicit view-mode modeling: Rather than leaving perspectives implicit in text captions [9, 38, 40, 59], we explicitly incorporate discrete view tokens (FREE, FPP, and TPP) into the context. Joint training across these regimes distinguishes their motion semantics, while enabling in-video view switching to emerge naturally. Joint action-camera modeling: We jointly incorporate discrete actions and continuous camera trajectories into the context. Crucially, beyond their necessary separation in TPP interaction, we further study the less-examined FPP and FREE regimes, where camera trajectories often stand in for both forms of control [15, 31, 39]. Our analysis reveals complementary roles: action governs local command fidelity, whereas camera anchors global trajectory stability. Built upon ICC, World-in-Context natively captures cross-condition dependencies within unified attention space. While in-context tokens specify what controls are present at individual frames, naive token conditioning can still leave the dynamic evolution between distant moments to be modeled implicitly. To this end, we further introduce IT-RoPE (Interaction-Transport RoPE), lightweight positional encoding that incorporates pairwise control transitions directly into temporal attention. By jointly modeling control conditions and their temporal evolution, World-in-Context supports coherent interaction across viewing regimes and makes effective use of interactive supervision, with increasing benefits as controls become richer. More broadly, it reframes multicondition interaction as context modeling, offering unified interface for interactive world modeling. To summarize, this work contributes threefold: We introduce In-Context Conditioning (ICC) for interactive world modeling and present World-in-Context, which represents view, action, and camera controls as tokens within shared attention space, providing unified interface for diverse interaction signals. We investigate the often-overlooked roles of viewing regimes and joint action-camera control, revealing distinct view-dependent dynamics, emergent view switching, and complementary action-camera roles in command fidelity and trajectory stability. Extensive experiments on WBench demonstrate World-in-Context-5B matches 22B the that EchoWM in navigation (81.5 vs. 81.6) and substantially outperforms existing 5B baselines in perspective switching (93.8% vs. 18.8%). Controlled studies further confirm compounding gains of World-in-Context under richer controls, favorable sample efficiency, and causal applicability. 2. Related Work Interactive Video World Models. Interactive world models extend video generation toward closed-loop interaction, where future observations evolve according to user-steered conditions [3, 6, 32, 36, 45]. Following recent formulations [28, 43], existing mod- (i) How els mainly navigate two core dimensions: the world is viewed. Interactive environments span FREE, FPP, and TPP regimes. Prior works [9, 38, 39, 55] typically subsume them into shared camera formulation, leaving perspective implicit in text captions and often conflating FREE roaming with FPP motion. We instead explicitly condition on discrete view modes, distinguishing their physical motion semantics and naturally enabling dynamic view switching. (ii) How user inputs affect its evolution. Existing 2 Figure 2. unifies controls through ICC and models their temporal evolution with IT-RoPE. (Left) Prior methods use implicit view descriptions and separate control pathways. (Right) World-in-Context systems rely almost exclusively on continuous camera trajectories for navigation [9, 13, 31, 39, 55, 59] for all view modes, which inevitably entangles character and camera dynamics in TPP. To incorporate richer signals, recent approaches either formulate unified action interface across different regimes [19], or inject actions and camera poses through distinct architectural pathways [36]. Differing from these paradigms, we explicitly maintain view modes and represent character actuation alongside camera motion as jointly contextualized controls within the same attention space, effectively treating them as coexisting yet independent degrees of freedom. In-Context Conditioning. In-context learning, originally developed for language models [7], has increasingly been explored in visual generation. Prompt Diffusion [44] first enables diffusion models to infer visual tasks from contextual examples, followed by works that exploit shared attention contexts for taskagnostic or unified image generation [16, 17, 37, 46, 50]. This paradigm has recently extended to video through spatial or temporal in-context generation [8, 21], unified multimodal conditioning with full attention [12, 20], and reference videos as semantic prompts [2]. IC-World [47] further explores in-context generation for shared world modeling, focusing on consistency across multiple observations of the same world. In this work, we extend in-context conditioning to interactive video world modeling. 3. The world modeling space is organized around two complementary pillars: (i) how the world is viewed across perspectives, and (ii) how user inputs steer dynamics through concurrent character action and camera viewport movement. Unified In-Context Conditioning. Instead of introducing specialized parameter pathways for each control modality, all interactive signals are projected into unified sequence of condition tokens R𝐿𝑐 𝐷, matching the backbone hidden dimension 𝐷: = (cid:2)cview ; caction ; ccamera(cid:3), (4) where [ ; ] denotes concatenation along the sequence dimension. (5) Ingesting all controls into the shared self-attention allows cross-condition dependencies to be captured natively without ad-hoc modules, reframing interactive expansion into an in-context modeling problem. Decomposing Interactive Context. The condition sequence of World-in-Context explicitly decouples the interactive degrees of freedom: View Mode (cview): Disentangles FREE, FPP, and TPP regimes via learned categorical tokens, mitigating view ambiguity and naturally supporting dynamic switching. Action (caction): Encodes hybrid keyboard-action inputs to govern local character actuation, providing responsive command dynamics. Camera (ccamera): Embeds relative 6-DoF camera poses and Plücker coordinates to ensure continuous trajectory tracking and viewpoint stability. To complement in-context conditioning, we further incorporates geometric transport into the temporal attention mechanism to preserve continuous physical transitions across frames. The subsequent sections elaborate on the explicit view-mode formulation (4.2), examine joint action-camera decoupling (4.3), and introduce IT-RoPE for parameterized temporal attention (4.4). 4.2. Further details of transport accumulation and attention computation are provided in Section A.3. 4.5. Training of World-in-Context Training Data. We train World-in-Context on compact set of 100K video clips covering FREE, FPP, and TPP viewing regimes, accompanied by temporally aligned view, action, and camera annotations when available. While joint training across these single-regime clips naturally facilitates view-mode transitions (as analyzed in Section 4.2), we additionally incorporate small fraction of cross-view switching clips (500 sequences) with dynamic view schedules to reinforce transition stability. Training Protocol. Following the conditional flowmatching objective, World-in-Context undergoes bidirectional finetuning where video and control tokens jointly interact in the shared attention manifold. This bidirectional setup serves as our default configuration to benchmark the core in-context conditioning paradigm. In Section 6, we further investigate World-in-Context under broader operational settings, including causal rollout with in-context history and expanded game-control signals. 5. Analysis of In-Context Conditioning To further examine how conditioning strategies scale with input complexity, we compare ICC with additive injection [19] and AdaLN modulation [40] under progressively richer inputs with our same data: view (V), action (A), and camera (C). Obs.❺ Tracking intervening control evolution improves interactive attention. Compared to 3DIT-RoPE enhances both NAVIGATION RoPE, (80.5 81.2) and INTERACTION (86.2 86.8). While action transport sharpens command responsiveness and camera transport stabilizes spatial tracking, their combination delivers the most balanced performance. Moreover, full IT-RoPE clearly outperforms the endpoint-only variant (80.5/86.6), confirming that accumulating the intervening control sequence provides critical dynamics missed by endpoint offsets alone. 5.5. Analysis of Data Efficiency Our default interaction-training set comprises modest 100K navigation clips and 500 switching sequences. Since training-data scales are not consistently disclosed by existing methods, we assess data efficiency through controlled comparisons in Figure 13: 50K+250, 100K+500, and 125K+750. We summarize our observations as follows: Figure 11. Conditioning strategy analysis. ICC increasingly benefits the coordination of diverse controls as conditioning becomes richer. C/A/V denote camera/action/view. Obs.❹ ICCs advantage scales with conditioning richness. As shown in Figure 11, with camera control alone, ICC performs on par with alternative strategies (76.3 vs. 76.3-77.0). Its gains emerge under joint action-camera inputs (+0.6 in NAVIGATION, +1.1 in INTERACTION) and expand further when adding explicit view tokens (+1.0 and +1.4, reaching 81.2 and 86.8). These widening margins indicate that shared attention space coordinates diverse controls more effectively than separate injection pathways as interaction becomes compositional. Figure 13. Data scaling analysis. ICC consistently outperforms additive injection across training budgets. Obs.❻ ICC demonstrates data efficiency across scaling regimes. ICC consistently outperforms additive injection across all data regimes, especially in perspective switching. With only 50K+250 clips, ICC achieves 75.0% switching rate, already surpassing additive injection trained on twice the data (71.9% at 100K+500). At 100K+500, ICC exceeds the largest-budget additive baseline (125K+750) in both NAVIGATION (81.5 vs. 80.3) and SWITCH (93.8% vs. 78.1%), showing that shared in-context tokens make substantially more efficient use of interactive supervision. 12 Figure 14. Causal Modeling with In-Context History To examine the architectural extensibility of incontext conditioning beyond bidirectional generation, World-in-Context is naturally adapted to streaming causal rollouts. Following common causal training paradigms in interactive generation [60], the model is trained autoregressively to predict future frame latents conditioned on historical context. Rather than relying on external KV cache retrieval mechanisms, WiC-Causal directly incorporates historical latents into the shared self-attention sequence. Specifically, the condition sequence in Eq. As shown in Table 2, WiC-Causal exhibits competitive interactive performance, attaining an average NAVIGATION score of 81.2 and 90.6% FPPTPP success rate on WBench. Compared to the bidirectional counterpart (81.5 and 93.8%), causal modeling incurs negligible degradation while retaining better performance margin over existing 5B baselines. Furthermore, qualitative rollouts in Figure 15 demonstrate that WiC-Causal preserves long-horizon spatial coherence across diverse viewing regimes. Notably, in loopclosure and viewpoint reappearance scenarios (e.g., returning to previously explored landscapes or room corners), WiC-Causal consistently reproduces previously observed visual landmarks and layouts. 6.2. Scaling to Rich Game Controls To further demonstrate the extensibility and tokenlevel composability beyond canonical navigation commands, we extend World-in-Context to accommodate richer, high-frequency gameplay actions. Experiments are conducted on Counter-Strike 2 gameplay sequences from EWM [29]. To assess sample efficiency and generalizability, WiC-Game is trained on compact subset of single map (i.e., DUST II), and tested on unseen layouts as well as real-world scenarios. Specifically, the condition sequence is augmented with discrete game-control tokens: (cid:2)cfire ; cduck ; cwalk(cid:3), (12) corresponding to firing (weapon dynamics and muzzle flashes), crouching (viewport descent), and slow walking (motion attenuation), respectively. As illustrated in Figure 14, WiC-Game demonstrates sensitive, decoupled control execution across three complementary regimes: (i) In-domain: new control trajectories within the training map (DUST II) exhibit (ii) Out-of-distribution: instant actuation responses; when applied to unseen game maps (e.g., MIRAGE, NUKE), the model preserves scene consistency while faithfully following concurrent actions; (iii) Real-world transfer: using synthetic starting images, the learned actuation dynamics generalize naturally to realistic visual environments. and global stability. Augmented with IT-RoPE to encode accumulated control progression in temporal attention, World-in-Context achieves competitive navigation on WBench (81.5) matching the 22B EchoWM, while establishing strong perspectiveswitching capability (93.8%). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages under richer conditioning, favorable sample efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts, highlighting shared context modeling as scalable interface for interactive world simulation. rather interactive conditioning, of This Report. This work Positioning focuses primarily on the algorithmic formulation than trainof ing an all-encompassing system artifact, with World-in-Context serving as concrete instantiation of this design. The overall capacity of an interactive world model naturally depends on data quality, model size, and training scale. We use modest interaction-training set of 100K navigation clips and 500 switching sequences. Since comparable training-data statistics are not consistently disclosed by existing methods, we omit cross-method dataInstead, we scale comparisons from the main table. prioritize controlled comparisons that isolate the architectural advantages of shared context modeling and control-aware temporal attention, including their Specifeffectiveness across training-data budgets. ically, this work centers around three foundational control modalities, i.e., view mode, character action, and camera motion, as they directly address the core dimensions governing interactive navigation: how the environment is viewed across perspectives and how user inputs steer character actuation alongside viewport evolution. These algorithmic findings complement concurrent advances in scaling, presenting an extensible interface for coordinating diverse interactive controls.

Training Details of World-in-Context A.1. Training Data Data Sources. The training mixture comprises default collection of 100K single-regime navigation clips alongside subset of 500 FPPTPP switching sequences. All qualitative evaluation scenes presented in this work are strictly held out from the training set. Navigation Data (100K): Clips are collected across widely-adapted open-source video datasets, including DL3DV [27], RealEstate [58], Sekai [25], SpatialViD [42], EgoExo [34], and ABot-WorldExplorer [19]. Switching Data (500): Viewpoint-transition sequences are collected from EgoExo [34] and internal data. Quality Pipeline. The raw video corpus is filtered through standard three-stage automated filtering pipeline: Scene/Shot Continuity: Following LingBot-World [40], TransNetV2 [35] is deployed to detect abrupt scene transitions and shot boundaries; segmented multi-shot videos are removed to retain strictly continuous navigation segments. Motion Filtering: Following Open-Sora [57] and SANA-Video [4], UniMatch [51] optical flow and VMAF metrics are evaluated to quantify dynamic motion magnitude. Clips displaying static stagnation or excessive motion blur/discontinuities are discarded. Aesthetic Assessment: Dover [48] is utilized to score perceptual aesthetics, eliminating clips compromised by severe compression artifacts, overexposure, or low visual fidelity. Crucially, for FPP sequences, body-induced periodic oscillations and head-bobbing motions are decoupled and filtered out before discrete action discretization. that World-State Captioning. Unlike existing world- (e.g., LingBot-World [40], modeling frameworks Matrix-Game 3.0 [45]) synthesize verbose temporal narratives or dense temporal captions, World-in-Context adopts simplified world-state captioning formulation. Under the premise that generative world models should decouple scene constitution from action-driven exploration, captions in this pipeline exclusively summarize the static visual constitution of the environment (e.g., atmospheric conditions, spatial geometry, and layout entities). Conditioning Schema To facilitate versatile interactive control while accommodating constraints, World-in-Context adopts two-stage training curriculum and mixed-control schema across viewing regimes. annotation practical Control Annotation. The control signals mainly used in World-in-Context, i.e., view, camera, and action, are annotated as follows: View Mode: vision-language foundation model (i.e., Qwen3-VL-32B [1]) classifies clips into FREE, FPP, and TPP regimes. FREE is characterized by unconstrained, smooth aerial or camera roaming (e.g., drone cinematography); FPP captures embodied locomotion or in-cockpit perspectives; TPP encompasses external character-following camera arrangements. Ambiguous instances at boundaries are cross-verified and resolved using reconstructed camera trajectory statistics. Camera Trajectories: Following common practice, continuous 6-DoF camera trajectories and Plücker ray parameters are reconstructed using ViPE [14]. Action Inversion: While authentic character actuation natively originates from game-engine telemetry, obtaining massive synchronized game recordFigure 16. View distribution across two stages. Two-Stage Training Curriculum. As outlined in Section 4.5, training proceeds in two sequential phases (Figure 16): ➀ Stage-1 (General Navigation): World-in-Context is trained on 100K single-regime navigation clips to learn fundamental physical dynamics and interactive responsiveness across FREE, FPP, and TPP modes. 1 ➁ Stage-2 (Switching Consolidation): Rather than fine-tuning solely on switching data, World-in-Context constructs an 8K curriculum by mixing regular navigation clips with the 500 switching sequences, where switching clips are oversampled to reinforce transition stability while preserving base navigation capabilities. Figure 17. Action/camera distribution across two stages. Mixed Action-Camera Conditioning. In Section 4.3, joint training refers precisely to the composite conditioning mixture illustrated in Figure 17, rather than strictly enforcing concurrent dual signals on every training instance. In real-world data, simultaneously obtaining robust annotations for both modalities is often impractical; for instance, loose camera-following in TPP sequences complicates clean action discretization, and synthetic scenes can introduce camera pose estimation artifacts. Therefore, World-in-Context trains across composite conditioning mixture of action-only, camera-only, joint, and unconditioned samples. Distribution Transparency. The mixture schedules in Figure 16 and Figure 17 are reported for empirical transparency rather than claimed as an optimal configuration, reflecting practical trade-offs against data availability. Crucially, all comparative baselines (e.g., additive injection and AdaLN modulation in Section 5) follow this identical conditioning schema to guarantee strictly controlled architectural comparisons. B. Experimental Details B.1. Evaluation Benchmark We evaluate World-in-Context on WBench [54], benchmark for interactive video world models comprising 289 cases and 1, 058 interaction turns. Each case provides an initial image, world description, and multi-turn control sequences. We use its NAVIGATION split and FPPTPP perspective-switching subset. Navigation Suite. WBench benchmarks trajectoryfollowing navigation across five core dimensions: Quality: Assesses perceptual aesthetics, visual fidelity, motion dynamics, temporal flickering, and inter-frame motion smoothness. 2 Setting: Measures contextual adherence to the specified prompt, including scene appearance preservation, environmental style consistency, and subject persistence. Interaction: Evaluates motion responsiveness and command fidelity by comparing estimated camera trajectories with action-derived reference trajectories under translational, rotational, and symmetric steering commands. Setup of Analysis in Section 5 Additive injection and AdaLN modulation are reimplemented following the conditioning strategies of ABot-World [19] and LingBot-World [9], respectively. For explicit view conditioning in these baselines, the categorical view mode is embedded at each latent timestep, spatially broadcast, and fused with the available action and camera representations. The resulting composite features are added directly to the visual patch tokens for additive injection, or projected to predict affine modulation parameters for AdaLN. In 5.3 and 5.4, the default World-in-Context is evaluated prior to stage-2 switching consolidation to demonstrate the core architectural advantages of incontext conditioning and transport modeling.
